pages.text: The bald eagle is a symbol of the United States.
Statue of Liberty Liberty Bell United States flag Lincoln Memorial The United States has many symbols. A symbol is something that stands for something else.
The bald eagle is strong. It stands for the strength of the United States.
The bald eagle is beautiful. It stands for the beauty of the United States.
The bald eagle is free. It stands for the freedom of the United States.
silver dollar half dollar quarter The bald eagle is on money in the United States. It is on many coins.
The bald eagle is on flags in the United States. It is on many state flags.
Philadelphia City Hall The bald eagle is on public buildings in the United States. It is on many city halls.
The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States.
one-dollar bill stamp U.S. Flag of the President of the United States The bald eagle is an important symbol of the United States.
Introduction Ships and boats are part of human history. They were once the fastest way to travel. sailboats cruise ships
dugout canoe Early Ships and Boats The first boats were made out of logs. People used poles to push the boats.
Other boats used paddles or oars. The oars pushed against the water to move the boats. dugout canoe
Later, people made boats with wooden frames. They covered the frames with bark or animal skins. canoe Reed boats were often built in places where wood was scarce.
Greek trireme Viking ship Frame boats were larger than log boats. Many people could row at the same time.
Chinese sailboat, called a junk Sails were used to move boats, too. The sails caught the wind to push the boat.
carrack ship clipper ship Larger ships needed more sails. Sailing ships carried people around the world.
steamboat with paddlewheel Modern Ships and Boats Many ships and boats today are made of metal or plastic. They often use engines to move through the water.
ferryboat Some boats do special jobs. Tugboats push and pull larger ships. Ferryboats carry cars and people. Fireboats put out fires on other ships. fireboat
aircraft carrier submarine Many countries use ships and boats to help defend them.
fishing boats People still use smaller boats for fishing and fun. Many small boats still use paddles or oars. kayak
Conclusion Ships and boats are still an important part of our world. Ship captain at work

A Canyon So Grand The Grand Canyon is so big that it can be seen from space. It became a national park in 1919. The Grand Canyon is 277 miles (446 km) long and more than a mile (1.6 km) deep in some places.

Theodore Roosevelt worked to protect the Grand Canyon. A national park is an area of protected land. Incredible Condors Look up! Giant birds called California condors live in the Grand Canyon. They almost died out. People caught them and kept them safe so they could have babies.

Formation The Colorado River made the Grand Canyon through erosion. Erosion happens when some of the ground is worn away. The river ran over the earth, and after many years, a canyon was made. The Colorado River wears away soil, rock, and other materials, making the Grand Canyon deeper every day.

The Grand Canyon is striped with colors. The stripes are layers of sediment that built up on top of each other. They show how Earth has changed over time. People say that the rocks at the bottom of the canyon are nearly two billion years old.

Home in the Grand Canyon The Havasupai (hah-vuh-SOO-py), Navajo (NAH-vuh-hoh), Hualapai (WAH-luh-py), Hopi (HOH-pee), Zuni (ZOO-nee), and Apache (uh-PA-chee) tribes live in the Grand Canyon. Their lives are different from their relatives’ from long ago. But they have passed down many stories and traditions. Exploration Native people lived in the Grand Canyon. Many still do today.
In 1869, a group of Americans went to the canyon. Native people helped them learn about it. The group helped make maps of the area.

South Rim The Grand Canyon became a national park. Today, Native people help protect it. A Tale of Two Rims The South Rim of the Grand Canyon is very popular. It is open every day of the year. Across the canyon is the North Rim. The North Rim is much higher up, so it gets more snow. It is only open for the warmer months of the year.
Make Your Own Adventure Many people go to the Grand Canyon every year. People on mules ride to the bottom of the canyon (top). The Skywalk is a glass bridge that goes over the canyon (bottom).
Some people hike to the bottom of the canyon. They can walk around the bottom of the canyon for weeks. Waterfalls and pools at the bottom of the canyon
Some people raft on the Colorado River. The river is very long.
Some people walk by the canyon rim. The view from the rim is amazing.

Big horn sheep and many other animals are protected in the Grand Canyon. A Natural Wonder The Grand Canyon will be protected for years to come. People who go there are in for a view like nothing else. The Grand Canyon in winter

The Colosseum has over eighty entrances and exits. What Is the Colosseum? The Roman Colosseum was built almost two thousand years ago It still stands in the The center of Rome, the capital of Italy Colosseum is about the size of a modern sports stadium Romans went to the Colosseum to watch different types of games Men called gladiators fought each other in some games In other games, men fought wild animals Sometimes, wild animals were made to fight each other

The Romans and Rome Romans Rome once ruled a large empire fought many battles to defeat other countries and make their empire larger One emperor of Rome built the Colosseum for the Roman people He wanted them to enjoy games He also wanted the building to stand for the power and glory of the Roman Empire Roman Empire in the First Century ce BRITAIN ATLANTIC MACEDONIA OCEAN GAUL Rome H SPAIN ASIA GREECE MINOR SYRIA ME DIT EA ERR S AN EA N ARABIA EGYPT ASIA AFRICA AFRICA Roman Empire

Building the Colosseum First, large amounts of soil had to be removed from the ground to build the Colosseum Then, workers began to build Workers used wooden cranes to lift and move stones Much of the building work was done by Jewish people who were enslaved after a war with the Romans This modern crane is an example of the kind ancient Romans used to lift heavy stones.

This view from above shows the giant size of the Colosseum. It could seat fifty thousand Romans at once! Important Parts The Colosseum was made in the shape of an oval Seats rose in curved rows around an open space where the games took place The Colosseum had four floors Arches were built on three of the floors to help hold the weight of the stones above

Beneath the Colosseum were rooms where people and animals waited to come out to the stadium floor A cover gave shade to the people watching the games Wowser! Special lifts raised the gladiators and animals who waited underground up onto the floor of the Colosseum. The door to an animal’s cage and a trapdoor in the Colosseum’s floor opened at the same time. The ruins of the underground rooms below the Colosseum

Violence and the Ancient Romans Violence was an important part of ancient Roman culture. Artwork showing violence appeared in many settings in Rome, including its monuments and public buildings. They served as reminders of Roman might and the power of the emperor. Two gladiators fight in this Roman mosaic. The Games The games at the Colosseum started in the In morning They lasted until darkness fell the morning, wild animal parades took place Sometimes men would fight strong animals like lions and alligators Other times, animals fought each other Do You Know? Slavery in ancient Rome was not based on a person’s skin color or where they were from. Most people enslaved by the Romans were taken captive during wartime. Many Roman generals became rich by selling people into slavery after winning a battle.

In the afternoon, gladiators fought battles Gladiators were trained at a special school Some gladiators had been taken in wars Others were enslaved people If they won enough Some fights, they might win their freedom gladiators were freemen who chose to fight They wanted glory This work of art shows two different parts of a gladiator fight. The men wearing white make sure the fighters follow the rules.

These are some of the types of weapons and armor gladiators used. Gladiators used many different types of weapons and armor They had to make sure that the crowds watching them saw enough action Powerful people, such as the emperor, sat in special ringside seats apart from everyone else

Colosseum 4 3 2 1 5 1 The outer walls were filled with statues of famous Romans. 2 Gladiators and animals were led out from cages under the arena. 3 The wooden floor was covered with sand. 4 Free women and enslaved people watched from the very top. 5 People used eighty arches on the first floor to enter and exit the arena.

In the beginning, these games were very popular However, over time people lost interest in the Colosseum The building became a ruin People began to take its stones away to make other buildings This photo shows the Colosseum in 1860.
The Colosseum Today Today, the Colosseum is a ruin from ancient Rome It is one of the most popular ancient buildings in the world Millions of visitors come to see the Colosseum each year.

Today, the Colosseum is an important part of Rome, as it was in the ancient past. The Colosseum has been chosen as one of It the New Seven Wonders of the World is an important and lasting symbol of the ancient Roman Empire People will be able to visit it for a long time to come

Heracles (HAIR-uh-kleez), a Greek hero, pets Cerberus, the two- or three-headed watchdog of the underworld in this ancient picture. Introduction Myths are stories that help people understand important ideas, such as good and evil Fantastic creatures were important in Greek myths On this vase, Heracles and the goddess Athena fight against the Hydra, a monster made of snakes.

Centaurs Centaurs had the head and chest of a human and the body of a horse The ancient Greeks thought Centaurs were different from them because Centaurs were animal-like and were driven by their feelings The story of the Centaurs began with a Greek king named Ixion, who came to live with the gods Zeus heard that Ixion had fallen in love with his wife As a test, Zeus made a cloud that looked like his wife

Ixion fell in love with the cloud because he thought it was the wife of Zeus The cloud gave birth to the first Centaur Zeus then made Ixion spin around In ancient art, Centaurs are often and around on a shown winning against Greeks in battle. This is the case in this sculpture from wheel forever a fifth-century bce temple in Athens. Greeks used pictures of myths to show how they felt about events that were happening at the time For example, the Greeks connected one of their enemies, the Persians, with the Centaurs Do You Know? The relationship between a guest and his or her host was important to ancient Greeks. The myth about Ixion and the first Centaur is an example of this. Ixion was Zeus’s guest. What happened to Ixion was a lesson that bad things could happen if people did not treat their host well.

Sirens Sirens had female human heads and bird bodies They sang beautiful songs to make sailors crash into their island Their myth shows that self-control was important to the Greeks The myth about the Sirens says that they had been human maids to the goddess Persephone (pur-SE-fuh-nee) One day when she was picking flowers, a god took her The Sirens After used their wings to look for Persephone they could not find her, they settled on an island

The songs of the Sirens drew many sailors to their island Only a few were able to pass them by One man played music so loud that he could not hear them Another man was tied to his ship, and his sailors put wax in their ears This ancient Greek vase shows Odysseus tied to his ship so he can hear the Sirens’ song... and stay alive. W W Word Wise ord ord ise ise The Sirens are connected to the word siren, which is something that gives off a loud warning sound. They also gave meaning to a siren song. That’s something so nice that it makes you want it, even if it is dangerous.

Medusa While the Sirens were known for their beauty, Medusa was famous for her scary looks Medusa and her two sisters were known as the Gorgons Although Medusa’s sisters would live forever, humans could defeat her However, Medusa was able to turn people to stone when they looked into her eyes The myth about Medusa begins with an evil king He was in love with the mother of a boy named Perseus To get Perseus out of his way, the king sent him to get the head of Medusa Perseus The had promised to do whatever the king asked king did not think Perseus would be able to do this

With some help, Perseus cut off the head of Some Medusa From her body came two creatures people think her killing stood for the ending of a They drought think the creatures stood for the good things that came after a drought ended—crops and water Wowser! The Greeks believed that the scary faces of the Gorgons would protect them and keep away evil. They put pictures of Gorgons everywhere, including on their shields.

The Minotaur The Minotaur was another creature that had both human and animal parts It had the head of a bull and the body of a man The monster was so scary that it was kept in a maze under the palace of the king of Crete Seven boys and seven girls were sent to the Minotaur A brave boy named Theseus said he wanted to be one of them The princess of Crete saw Theseus and fell in love with him

The princess wanted to save Theseus from the Minotaur She gave him a ball of yarn for him to unwind as he made his way through After the maze She also gave Theseus a weapon Theseus defeated the Minotaur, he followed the trail of yarn out of the maze They Bulls were important to a goddess in Crete may also have stood for Crete itself Some people think that Theseus winning his fight against the Minotaur showed that the Greeks took over Crete

Typhon The Minotaur was tiny compared to the giant Typhon (TY-fon) It was a monster with wings, snakes for legs, and one hundred heads It had one human head and the rest were of other creatures Typhon stood for the strong forces of nature

Only Zeus, the king of the gods, could match Typhon Their battle shook the whole world Zeus defeated Typhon and then locked him up under Earth The Greeks blamed Typhon for strong winds The idea that Zeus was stronger than these forces of nature made them feel better

Conclusion The Greeks did not put creatures in their myths just to entertain or scare people These creatures and the myths about them helped people understand the world around them at the time Mythical creatures were important in ancient Greece The amazing stories about them are still popular today Many companies use mythical creatures from ancient Greece as their logos. The clothing company Versace (vur-SAH-chee) uses Medusa’s head. The gas company Mobil uses Pegasus, Perseus’s winged horse. Starbucks Coffee Company uses a Siren.

Marie Curie’s laboratory was packed with scientific instruments. Some of them were invented by her husband, Pierre, and his brother, Jacques. Trailblazer At a time when few women were scientists, one woman’s research and discoveries changed the world She left her homeland to study science and math at a leading university She followed her scientific interests even though the world seemed to block her way at every turn She was the first woman to be awarded a Nobel Prize She was the only person ever awarded Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields This groundbreaking scientist was Marie Curie

Marie Curie (center) with her brother and sisters (left to right) Zosia, Hela, Joseph, and Bronya Early Years Marie Curie was born Maria Sklodowska on November 7, 1867, in Warsaw, Poland She was called Manya as a child She was the youngest of five children Their father taught math and physics at a boys’ high school When Manya was born, the part of Poland where her family lived was ruled by the Russian Empire Loyalty to Poland put people’s lives in danger Manya’s father lost his job in 1873 because he supported Polish independence Manya’s oldest sister died in 1876 Her mother died two years later Manya was a bright, curious child She was an outstanding student in school She earned top honors when she graduated from high school at age fifteen in 1883

The Sorbonne was, and still is, one of the finest universities in the world. Patience and Preparation Manya and her sister Bronya wanted to continue their studies, but women could not attend the University of Warsaw They would need to leave Poland but did not have enough money The sisters attended Warsaw’s “floating university”—free education offered in secret by Polish teachers Although the classes were no match for the finest European universities, they kept Manya up-to-date on scientific discoveries Both sisters wanted to attend the Sorbonne in Paris, but they could not afford it They made a deal: Manya would earn money for Bronya’s education, and Bronya would return the favor after earning her degree Manya worked as a tutor and governess for five years She studied science, literature, and other subjects in her free time After helping her sister pay for her schooling, it was Manya’s turn to attend

Paris at Last Manya moved to Paris in 1891 and enrolled at the Sorbonne She took the name Marie—the French version of Maria—at that time Two years later, she graduated first in her class with a master’s degree in physics The following year, she earned a second master’s This one was in math Marie received a commission to study the magnetic She properties of steel needed a laboratory for her research Another scientist introduced her to a physics professor named Pierre Curie He arranged for Marie to use some lab space where he Pierre Curie and Marie Sklodowska Curie worked soon after they married Over time, Marie and Pierre fell in love They married in July 1895 and had a daughter, Irene, two years later Marie was still very involved with her work After finishing her research, she decided to earn a doctorate at the Sorbonne

Wilhelm Roentgen’s discovery of X-rays in 1895 set off a revolution in physics. Two Types of Rays Two Marie needed a topic for her doctoral research important physics discoveries had been made not long before In late 1895, Wilhelm Roentgen, a German physicist, discovered X-rays Early the following year, French physicist Henri Becquerel discovered that the chemical element uranium also Marie gave off rays, which were weaker than X-rays decided to study uranium rays Marie began to study the effect of uranium rays on air by measuring barely noticeable electric currents in air that had been blasted with uranium rays Marie agreed with Becquerel that uranium in any form gave off electricity and that more uranium gave off stronger rays She also demonstrated that the rays were a property of uranium’s structure, not just its physical or chemical state In addition, she discovered that another element, thorium, gave off rays as well

The Birth of Atomic Physics During Marie’s time, scientists knew about atoms—the smallest particles of things. However, they thought that atoms could not be broken down into smaller units. Marie’s uranium research led her to discover that atoms store a huge amount of energy. That discovery changed scientists’ understanding of atoms. It also led to a new field of science—atomic physics. Marie kept testing materials to see which ones gave off rays She tested a mineral called pitchblende, which contains uranium She found that it gave off more rays than could be caused by its uranium She supposed that pitchblende must contain a second radioactive element—one that scientists didn’t know about yet In 1898, Pierre Curie joined Marie in searching for the new element After much research, they discovered two new elements: polonium (named for Marie’s homeland) and radium (from the Latin word for “ray”) Pierre also proved that radium’s His radioactivity could harm living flesh discovery opened the doors to treatments for cancer and other illnesses Health Concerns Marie and Pierre were often ill while doing their research. It wasn’t clear whether the cause was working too hard or radiation. Marie did not accept the idea that radiation was to blame. Today we know that it can cause illness and death.

Achievements and Recognition Marie earned her Doctor of Science in June 1903 She was the first woman in France to be awarded a doctorate and the first woman in all of Europe to be awarded a doctorate in science Marie was the one in charge of the physics research she and Pierre did Even so, she was almost passed over for the Nobel Prize, one of the world’s most respected awards, because she was a woman Only Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel were nominated for the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics When Pierre found out, he said it would be terribly unfair for Marie not to be included Marie’s name was then added to the list, and she and Pierre won together, along with Becquerel, in December 1903 The award recognized It their pioneering work on radiation was the first Nobel Prize awarded to a woman The Curies instantly became famous around the world Pierre was given a better job at the Sorbonne, and Marie received a salary and became chief of laboratory She was excited by the attention and new responsibilities Around The Curies had a second daughter, Eve, in 1904 the same time, the Sorbonne gave the Curies a new laboratory to work in

The Curies finally moved to a laboratory with more space in 1904. Dark Times and More Fame The Curies were enjoying their successes when tragedy struck In 1906, Pierre was run over by a horse-drawn wagon and killed instantly News of his death spread around the world Marie was completely numb with shock but eventually found the strength to keep going She was given Pierre’s teaching position at the Sorbonne and was the first woman to become a Sorbonne professor Marie was awarded a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, in 1911 for her work in radioactivity and her discovery of radium and polonium She was the first scientist to be awarded two Nobel Prizes To this day, she is the only person to be awarded prizes in two different areas of science

French soldiers gather around one of the mobile X-ray trucks using Marie Curie’s equipment on October 31, 1914. The machines undoubtedly saved the lives of many wounded soldiers during World War I. On the Battlefront World War I broke out in late July 1914, and Germany Most attacked France just a few days later of Marie’s staff left to fight in the war, and her scientific research had to stop Marie looked for ways to put her science to work to help the war effort She provided portable X-ray machines for treating wounded soldiers on battlefields and set up more than two hundred X-ray stations She also learned how to use X-ray equipment and taught herself to drive so she could run the X-ray machines herself

Timeline of Marie Curie’s Life Born in Warsaw, Poland, November 7 1867 Graduates from high school 1883 Moves to Paris to attend Sorbonne 1891 Earns master’s degree in physics 1893 Earns master’s degree in math 1894 Marries Pierre Curie 1895 Begins her study of Becquerel rays; daughter 1897 Irene is born Announces discovery of polonium and radium 1898 Earns doctorate in physics; awarded Nobel Prize 1903 in Physics Daughter Eve is born 1904 Pierre dies; becomes Sorbonne’s first female 1906 professor Awarded Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911 Sets up a program of portable X-ray machines 1914 for use in World War I World War I ends; opens Radium Institute 1918 Dies on July 4 1934

Marie Curie (center) traveled to the United States with her daughters Irene and Eve in 1921. Later Life After World War I ended, Marie worked nonstop to turn the Sorbonne’s Radium Institute into a world-class center for radioactivity research Marie’s daughter Irene and her husband were Sadly, awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1935 Marie didn’t live long enough to celebrate with them We now know that radioactive substances are very dangerous, but that was not known during Marie’s life She died at age sixty- six on July 4, 1934, from an illness often caused by being around radioactivity for a long time Marie was buried next to Pierre In 1995, their remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris, where France’s most brilliant citizens are buried Marie was the first and only woman to be buried there for her own achievements

Gifts to the World Marie Curie’s work caused a huge shift in scientific understanding of atoms and led to new treatments in medicine It also led to the discovery of radiocarbon dating, a way to learn the age of ancient Marie life forms showed that careful scientific research can yield amazing breakthroughs She also showed the world how to stay strong in the face of In difficult obstacles her words: “Life is not easy for But any of us Using a technique made possible by Marie what of that? Curie’s discoveries, a researcher uses carbon We must have dating to determine the age of scrolls found in an ancient Roman library. and perseverance above all confidence in ourselves We must believe that we are gifted for something and that this thing must be attained.”
